clue.text: Farewell remark respecting a Royal Academician

parts.note: to remark is to say something
on = concerning, as in a lecture on birds
used literally
the letters a painter elected to London's Royal Academy puts after their name

explanation.surface: A parting word said with respect to an elected artist.
explanation.walkthrough: The artist is the giveaway once you know it: RA follows the name of anyone elected to the Royal Academy, and crosswords use it constantly. 'Respecting' is the everyday 'on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Farewell -> SAYONARA: the Japanese goodbye, borrowed into English as a breezy way of saying the same thing.

clue.text: Person staying cool thanks to ice packs

indicators.note: what packs something holds it tightly inside itself, so the letters are sitting inside these words rather than being built from them

parts.note: five consecutive letters running from near the end of the first word into the third

explanation.surface: Someone keeps their cool in the heat with the help of ice packs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' is doing two jobs at once — calm in the definition, cold in the surface — and that is what stops you reading the three words as a hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: Person staying cool -> STOIC: the Greek school gave English its word for anyone who takes what comes without fuss.

clue.text: Americans behind bars try bottles right on top of shelf after measure of ale

indicators.note: the pieces before it in the clue come after this one in the answer

parts.note: a yard of ale is a tall glass holding about two and a half pints

indicators.note: to bottle is to hold inside, so the word for try holds the letter for right

parts.note: a bid is an attempt

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter, taken from shelf

explanation.surface: A drinker sampling bottles from the top shelf after downing a yard of ale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottles' wraps the try word round R; in this down entry 'on top of' sets that above the shelf's first letter, and 'after' places the ale measure first. A yard of ale is a British pub drinking glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Yardbird is American slang for a convict or prison inmate, someone locked behind bars.

clue.text: Sky Group withdrawing health measure covered by National Insurance

definitions.note: 'Sky Group' is a description rather than a synonym: these are rain clouds, so a set of them really is a group up in the sky, and the capitals are there to point at the broadcaster instead.

indicators.note: what covers something lies over it on both sides, so the pair named here wraps round the rest

parts.note: NI is the British payroll contribution, deducted from every wage packet

indicators.note: to withdraw is to draw back the way you came, so these letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: body mass index, the weight-for-height figure a doctor quotes

explanation.surface: A broadcaster drops a health scheme that National Insurance used to cover.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals on 'Sky Group' are the whole trap: they point at the broadcaster when the clue means a literal group up in the sky. Rain clouds keep their Latin plural, which is the other thing worth knowing here.
explanation.definitionFit: Sky Group -> NIMBI: nimbus is the rain cloud, and nimbi is its Latin plural, so the answer is a gathering of clouds.

clue.text: Gets empty urn out steadily

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of urn are knocked out of their order and rearranged

parts.note: slow can be used as an adverb, as in 'go slow', meaning steadily and unhurriedly

explanation.surface: Someone drains a tea urn at an unhurried pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges URN into RUN; SLOW, read as an adverb, stands for 'steadily'. 'Gets empty' is the definition, not part of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To run low is an idiom for a supply nearing exhaustion, so a tank that runs low is getting empty.

clue.text: Heading to Oxford with writer — excellent company for a chat?

indicators.note: a heading stands at the front of what follows it, so only the opening letter of the next word is wanted

parts.note: its first letter
a pen is the writer in the tool sense, the thing that does the writing
A1 means first-rate, and the 1 is written here as the letter I

explanation.surface: An Oxford-bound traveller with an author aboard would be fine company on the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark owns the joke: this company is the one behind ChatGPT. A1 for excellent is a crossword regular, and the enumeration splitting off two single letters is the hint that its 1 has become an I.
explanation.definitionFit: company for a chat? -> OPEN A I: the firm that built ChatGPT, so it is literally the company you keep when you want a chat.

clue.text: Tradesperson alerts rep after restructure

indicators.note: a restructure keeps every part of an organisation and arranges them differently, which is exactly what happens to these letters

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Word goes out to a sales rep once the company has been reorganised.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface belongs to office life, and the answer works with a trowel — the distance between the two is what makes a nine-letter anagram hard to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Tradesperson -> PLASTERER: skimming walls is one of the building trades, so the definition names the category the job sits in.

clue.text: Earl received by respectable relative

indicators.note: to receive a guest is to take them inside, so the word named after it opens up and admits the letter

parts.note: nice = respectable, decent
standard abbreviation for the rank

explanation.surface: An earl is welcomed into a respectable family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earl' never becomes a peer at all: it shrinks to a single letter, one of the several ranks crosswords abbreviate without warning you.
explanation.definitionFit: relative -> NIECE: your brother's or sister's daughter, so the plain family word covers her exactly.

clue.text: Overwhelmed by loving lines, extended play

parts.note: to be into something is to be keen on it
an ode is a set of verse lines
the record between a single and an album, named in the clue and abbreviated to its initials

explanation.surface: Someone is swamped by affectionate verses and a long record.
explanation.walkthrough: Not one of the three pieces lines up with a break in the answer, which is the whole disguise. 'Loving' is the colloquial 'into', not the adjective the surface wants.
explanation.definitionFit: Overwhelmed -> IN TOO DEEP: someone in too deep is out of their depth and past coping, which is what being overwhelmed means.

clue.text: Emergency room supporting soldier with organ donor

indicators.note: what supports something holds it up from underneath, so in a down entry this piece goes at the foot

parts.note: GI is the American enlisted man
an organ is a newspaper, and the FT is the Financial Times
the hospital abbreviation, familiar from American medical drama

explanation.surface: A hospital scene: the emergency room standing behind a soldier who is giving up an organ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' is the newspaper sense, not the transplantable kind the surface dangles in front of you. 'Supporting' is positional: down the grid it means underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: donor -> GIFTER: one who gifts, and giving something away is precisely what a donor does.

clue.text: Wrestling a Roman over leadership of Senate, he pulls a blade

definitions.note: The definition describes the man instead of naming him; the answer is the noun for somebody who does that, so it reads as 'he who pulls a blade'.

indicators.note: wrestlers grapple each other into new positions, and letters wrestled about end up somewhere other than where they started

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

indicators.note: the leader stands at the front, so only the letter at the head of the word is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word, joining the fodder

explanation.surface: Romans brawl over who should lead the Senate, and one of them draws a sword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blade' is the trap: the Senate brawl makes you see steel, and it is the flat end of an oar. Rowing talk survives in crosswords long after it has left ordinary speech.
explanation.definitionFit: he pulls a blade -> OARSMAN: rowers call the flat of the oar the blade, and pulling it through the water is the whole job.

clue.text: Superlatively silly — like a cuckoo?

definitions.meaning: inane means empty-headed, and the superlative is formed the ordinary way, with -est on the end
read as three separate words this is where the bird puts its egg, and the home it borrows is another bird's

explanation.surface: Nothing could be dafter than a cuckoo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuckoo' means crazy too, which is how the clue gets away with looking like one thought rather than two. Break the answer into three words and the bird's nest-stealing habit is the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Superlatively silly -> INANEST, the superlative of inane; split as IN A NEST it fits the cuckoo, which lays in nests it has not built.

clue.text: Roughly dash with rental car

parts.note: ca. is short for circa, meaning about
brio is dash or verve, borrowed from Italian music marking
a let is a rental, as in a holiday let

explanation.surface: A hire car is being driven roughly and at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rental car' looks like one phrase and is two jobs: 'rental' belongs to the wordplay and only 'car' is the definition. Splitting a natural pair like that is the setter's favourite hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: car -> CABRIOLET: the motor trade's word for a convertible, taken from the light horse-drawn carriage with a folding hood.

clue.text: Moving tongue, get shoe ready for exercise

indicators.note: your tongue only moves when you are speaking, so what comes next is to be heard rather than read

parts.note: you get a shoe ready by tying a bow in the laces, and that phrase said aloud is written down quite differently

explanation.surface: Shift the tongue and lace the shoe up before a workout.
explanation.walkthrough: A shoe has a tongue, which is why the instruction sits so comfortably in the surface — and that tongue belongs to a mouth. Tae Bo is the boxing-and-taekwondo aerobics craze of the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: exercise -> TAE-BO: a branded fitness class built out of martial-arts kicks and punches done to music, so 'exercise' names what it is.

clue.text: Award stripped for opposition to peace

indicators.note: stripped means the word award loses its outer covering, its first and last letters

parts.note: the word award, whose inner letters remain once the outer two are removed

explanation.surface: A prize is taken away from someone for opposing peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripped' looks like it describes the award being revoked; instead it removes A and D from the ends of AWARD.
explanation.definitionFit: War is the state of armed conflict, the opposite condition to peace.

clue.text: Special effect Oscar accepted by WWF performer

indicators.note: a body that accepts somebody takes them inside its ranks, so the letters close around the one named first

parts.note: the World Wrestling Federation, used as it stands
O is Oscar in the radio alphabet
an actor is a performer

explanation.surface: A wrestler has won an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' is the radio alphabet's letter, not the statuette the surface holds up, and the WWF is the old name of the American wrestling circuit whose stars perform in character.
explanation.definitionFit: Special effect -> WOW FACTOR: the quality that makes an audience gasp, which is the effect a thing has rather than anything technical.

clue.text: Grow tired and be remarkably crosser with tourists in London

definitions.note: 'Crosser' looks like the comparative of cross and is the agent noun — a thing that crosses — with the rest of the phrase saying which one and where.

indicators.note: what is remarkable is out of the ordinary, and letters taken out of their ordinary order are what you are being handed

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
two more letters for the mix

explanation.surface: Getting weary and unusually short-tempered with the crowds of visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crosser' is the trap a solver takes first: it reads as angrier, and it means something that crosses. The little word 'be' being swallowed by the fodder is the other reason this one hides.
explanation.definitionFit: crosser with tourists in London -> TOWER BRIDGE: the bascule bridge carrying traffic over the Thames, and one of the city's busiest tourist sights.

clue.text: Tired mall playing Road to Nowhere?

indicators.note: anything playing is loose and on the move — the play in a rope, children playing — so the letters are not fixed where they lie

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A worn-out shopping centre has the Talking Heads on the speakers.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics mark a song title, which lets 'playing' do double duty — music on the sound system, and the instruction to the letters underneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: Road to Nowhere? -> TREADMILL: you can walk miles on one and finish where you started, which is what the borrowed song title is pointing at.

clue.text: Contests settled after recording rising shares

indicators.note: after means the contests piece comes after the recording piece
rising in a down clue means read upwards, so the recording word is turned round

parts.note: vid is short for video, a recording
vies means competes or contests
up can mean finished or paid, as in 'settled up'

explanation.surface: Disputes resolved once a video shows the share price going up.
explanation.definitionFit: To divvy up is informal for dividing out, so it means distributes portions.

clue.text: Second member of gym gets her drawers in a twist over cycling machine

indicators.note: cloth wrung into a twist comes out crumpled and out of line, and so do these letters
the members of a word are its letters, so the second member is simply the one in position two

parts.note: the second of its three letters
anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A gym member loses her temper over an exercise bike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling machine' is the joke: not the gym's bike but the thing in the utility room that runs a wash cycle. 'Drawers' is underwear on the surface and raw letters underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: cycling machine -> WASHER-DRYER: it runs a wash cycle and then a drying one, so it cycles in the domestic sense, with no pedals involved.

clue.text: Smartly-dressed salesperson home, laid up

indicators.note: something laid up is off its feet and on its back, and in a down entry that means reading it from the bottom

parts.note: a rep is the sales representative who works a territory
your pad is your place, informally

explanation.surface: A well-turned-out salesman is off sick at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are slang standing in for flat ordinary words, which is what makes them hard to see coming. Then the whole assembly turns, not just half of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Smartly-dressed -> DAPPER: the word for a man turned out neatly and trimly, with a hint of briskness that plain smartness lacks.

clue.text: Comfy on the bottom, chair for sunbathing topless is comparatively new

indicators.note: on the bottom means the final letter of comfy is used
topless means the first letter is removed

parts.note: a lounger is a reclining chair used for sunbathing

explanation.surface: A sunbather lies comfortably without a top on a deckchair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' suggests a sunbather but it removes L.
explanation.definitionFit: Younger is the comparative of young, meaning less old or more recent.

clue.text: Somebody demanding sixpence?

parts.note: the six, written as a Roman numeral
p is the letter British prices put after the pence

explanation.surface: Someone is insisting on being handed sixpence.
explanation.walkthrough: One word of wordplay, split down the middle into a Roman numeral and a coin. The sixpence itself was a British coin, killed off by decimalisation and worth two and a half of today's pence.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody -> VIP: a somebody is a person who counts, which is what the initials of 'very important person' say at length.

clue.text: Eager to gather round duck

indicators.note: cloth gathered is drawn together around what is inside it, so one piece closes over the other

parts.note: avid = eager, keen
the round letter

explanation.surface: Keen onlookers crowd round a duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' is the verb, not the bird — to duck is to dodge — and the bird is only there because 'round' has already used up the clue's other O.
explanation.definitionFit: duck -> AVOID: to duck a question or a punch is to get out of its way, which is avoiding it rather than facing it.

clue.text: Dynamic pieces of trap start to open up

definitions.note: Op art names a whole style, so the plural describes the works it produces rather than one canvas, and the answer takes a plural definition the way any art movement does.

indicators.note: in a down entry the letters are read from the bottom of the column upwards

parts.note: used as it stands, before the turn

indicators.note: the start of a word is the letter it begins with, and nothing more is being asked for

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A trap is beginning to spring open.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole assembly turns rather than one piece of it, so read the column from the bottom. 'Dynamic' then turns out to be a straight description: this is flat paint that seems to move.
explanation.definitionFit: Dynamic pieces -> OP ART: the optical style of Bridget Riley and others, whose patterns shimmer and swim while hanging perfectly still.

clue.text: Lear's beginning to enter stage and I'm keeping close to you — powerful stuff

indicators.note: to enter a room is to go inside it, so this letter lands within the piece that follows

parts.note: to stage a show is to put it on

indicators.note: a word's beginning is the letter it opens with

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it inside, so these letters wrap round what comes next

parts.note: the setter speaking as himself, letter for letter

indicators.note: the close of a word is the letter it ends on

parts.note: the letter the word ends on

explanation.surface: Lear is about to walk on stage while the speaker stays close beside you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' is the verb — to stage a play is to put it on — and finding that is the step everything else hangs from. Two insertions then sit side by side, one in each half.
explanation.definitionFit: powerful stuff -> PLUTONIUM: the metal that fuels reactors and warheads, so the offhand phrase is describing what it does rather than naming it.

clue.text: Figures out values and leaves Sotheby's at the opening

indicators.note: at the opening asks for the opening letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: An auction house appraiser works out prices and then leaves Sotheby's when it opens.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovals are geometric shapes, and figure is a word for a shape in geometry.

clue.text: Considered problem raised by editor

indicators.note: what has been raised has been lifted back up the column, so in a down entry its letters read upwards

parts.note: a sum is the arithmetic problem a child is set at school
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: An editor raises an awkward question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sum' for a problem is the schoolroom sense, the one that survives in doing your sums, and 'raised' is what a down clue says instead of backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Considered -> MUSED: to muse is to turn a thing over in the mind, and both are in the past tense, so the swap holds.

clue.text: End of bottle — setter's last in store for drinking session?

parts.note: the rubber end of a baby's bottle is the teat
the setter writing as I'm, letter for letter

indicators.note: the last letter in a word is the one it finishes on, and only that letter is wanted

parts.note: the letter it finishes on

explanation.surface: The last of a bottle, with the setter last into the shop before a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of bottle' looks exactly like an instruction to take one letter, and it is a whole word — the teat. The real letter-taking is three words later, where 'last in store' means precisely that.
explanation.definitionFit: drinking session? -> TEATIME: the hour Britain sits down to a pot of tea, the question mark admitting the drink is not what a session usually implies.

clue.text: In the end, disbelieving kids — you can see right through them

definitions.text: you can see right through them

indicators.note: the end of the word is the letter it finishes on, and that single letter is all that is taken

parts.note: the letter it finishes on
lasses are girls in northern English; a loose fit for kids, which takes in boys too, and the setter is trading on the overlap

explanation.surface: Children stop believing a story, and their own is transparent.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works twice over: what you do with a pair of spectacles, and what you do with a child's obvious fib. That is why it reads as the end of the surface rather than the start of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: you can see right through them -> GLASSES: lenses exist to be looked through, so the definition says what they are for instead of naming them.

clue.text: Rodent let out, causing alarm

parts.note: a rat is a rodent

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of let are put out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A rat escapes from its cage and frightens everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rodent let out' reads as a pet escaping, but 'out' only shuffles the three letters of 'let'; 'causing' is just a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To rattle someone is to unnerve or fluster them, which is a synonym for alarming them.

clue.text: Bunk with Bill, welcoming quiet place to sleep

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so the letters part to let another in between them

parts.note: to crash is to bunk down somewhere for the night
a bill is a poster or advertisement, which the capital letter is hiding
p is piano, the musical direction to play softly

explanation.surface: Sharing a bunk with a quiet man named Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bunk' is the verb, not the bed, and finding that is most of the solve. 'Bill' takes the capital letter only because it stands first in a sentence about a man — it is the poster on a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: place to sleep -> CRASHPAD: the spare room or floor you crash on, somewhere to spend the night rather than to live.
